answer: The submission is honest, clear and well-organized, but it reads as a concept with caveats rather than an evidence-backed venture case. Priority improvements: (1) Quantify the problem and market. Replace 'several million' and 'a meaningful portion' with cited figures (e.g., prevalence of chronic conditions among 18-34s, cost-related nonadherence rates) and build a bottom-up TAM/SAM/SOM with an explicit initial beachhead (e.g., students at specific campuses). (2) Show traction, not just activity. 'Early comments' from a small group is weak. Report the number of users, usage frequency, retention, actual dollars saved per prescription, and 2-3 direct user quotes or a short survey result. Even a modest pilot with real savings numbers would materially strengthen the case. (3) Build a simple unit-economics model. Estimate referral fee per fill, fills per user per year, expected conversion to premium, CAC via campus channels, and data licensing cost per user. Show break-even scenarios and tie the $75K ask to a line-item budget with milestones and a runway/timeline. (4) Sharpen differentiation and defensibility. 'Young adults + budgeting + multi-source comparison' is easy for GoodRx, insurer apps or chains to copy. Explain what is hard to replicate: proprietary user data, campus/clinic distribution partnerships, a behavioral approach, or integrations. Include a competitor comparison table showing features, pricing and business model. (5) Address the model's core tension. Referral fees reward steering transactions, which can conflict with the stated goal of lowest price; explain how trust and neutrality are preserved, and show evidence (e.g., letters of intent or conversations) that discount providers or pharmacies will actually pay. (6) Treat regulation and privacy as a plan, not a mentorship request. State whether HIPAA applies, how health and medication data are stored, consent and data-minimization practices, and any state privacy law exposure; list the specific risks and your mitigation steps. (7) Strengthen team credibility. Identify specific relevant experience, formalize the faculty and pharmacist advisors (even as named advisors), and note any gaps (e.g., healthcare compliance, pharmacy-benefit expertise) and how they will be filled. (8) Validate secondary markets or cut them. Untested campus health, employer and clinic channels dilute focus; either add one signal of interest (a conversation or pilot commitment) or drop them. (9) Make the ask specific and measurable. Define success metrics for the pilot (e.g., 300 users, average savings per fill, 30/60-day retention, number of provider conversations) and what threshold would trigger a seed raise. (10) Tighten the writing. Cut hedging phrases ('we believe', 'we have not yet') in favor of stating what is known, what is being tested, and by when.
